lead: A voltage multiplier is a ladder of diodes and capacitors. Capacitors charge on one half-cycle and stack in series on the next, so the DC output is a multiple of the input peak Vp. Each diode–capacitor pair adds one Vp: a doubler uses two pairs (2Vp), a tripler three (3Vp), a quadrupler four (4Vp). The multiplication factor equals the number n of diode–capacitor pairs. No transformer is needed to reach a few hundred volts. Multipliers bias photomultiplier tubes, laser and X-ray heads, precipitators and older CRT anodes. They give high voltage at low current, and that current limit drives the design.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for rectifier action, Chapter 1.2 for capacitor charging and ripple, and Chapter 1.3 for the clamp that starts the ladder.

sections.h3: The clamp and the peak detector

blocks.text: A multiplier uses two diode–capacitor habits. A diode with a capacitor charges to Vp and holds it: a peak detector. Put that charged capacitor in series with the source and its Vp adds to the source, lifting the waveform by Vp: a clamp. A multiplier is a chain of clamps.

items: Negative half-cycle: D1 conducts, C1 charges to Vp with its left plate negative.
Positive half-cycle: source and C1 add, so D2 anode reaches about 2Vp.
D2 conducts and C2 charges to 2Vp; D1 is reverse biased.
The steps repeat every cycle; no-load output stays at 2Vp.

blocks.text: Two diodes and two capacitors give no-load 2Vp. This is the half-wave doubler.

sections.h3: From doubler to tripler and quadrupler

blocks.text: Add one diode and one capacitor and you add one more Vp. The new capacitor sits on the previous DC level. C3 charges to 3Vp through D3, and C4 to 4Vp through D4. A cascade of n pairs gives n·Vp at no load.

blocks.where: Vout is no-load DC output in volts; n is number of diode–capacitor pairs, also the multiplication factor (2 doubler, 3 tripler, 4 quadrupler); Vp is peak input in volts, not rms; Vd is one diode forward drop in volts.

blocks.text: A bridge or full-wave doubler uses two diodes and two capacitors, charging one capacitor on each half-cycle, so its ripple is at 2f. The cascade above is half-wave: charge reaches the output once per cycle. Only a few universities teach these cascade details.

Each pair adds a diode drop and series resistance, and charge arrives once per cycle. n·Vd is lost even at no load. On load the output falls further by resistive and charge-transfer drop, roughly I·R<sub>eff</sub>, where R<sub>eff</sub> is effective series resistance. For an n-pair half-wave cascade the ripple grows roughly as n(n+1)·I/(2fC); the one-pair value is ΔV ≈ I/(fC).

items: Ripple frequency is f (50 Hz from mains), not 2f, for the half-wave cascade.
Load regulation is poor; multipliers suit microamp to milliamp loads.

C1 has only Vp across it: rate it above Vp. D1 must withstand 2Vp in reverse. The doubler output capacitor C2 must be rated above 2Vp. In an n-pair ladder the last capacitor top plate stands at n·Vp above ground, so its rating and insulation must exceed n·Vp.
Design from peak values: a 10 V rms winding gives Vp = 14.1 V, not 10 V.

figure.caption: Each block adds a diode–capacitor pair. A 10 V peak input is clamped and pumped one Vp per pair to 20 V, 30 V or 40 V at no load.

spec.title: Multiplier ladder
spec.aria: Diode–capacitor ladder: 10 V peak input gives no-load outputs of 20 V, 30 V or 40 V.

examples.question: A cascade multiplier runs from a 10 V peak, 50 Hz source with ideal diodes. Find the no-load DC output of a doubler, tripler and quadrupler. Repeat the doubler with Vd = 0.7 V.
steps: Input is already peak: Vp = 10 V.
examples.answer: Ideal no-load outputs are 20 V, 30 V and 40 V; the doubler with 0.7 V diodes gives 18.6 V.
examples.check:
Vp = 10.0
Vd = 0.7
print(f"{2*Vp:.1f}")
print(f"{3*Vp:.1f}")
print(f"{4*Vp:.1f}")
print(f"{2*Vp - 2*Vd:.1f}")

traps: Using rms input as Vp: a 10 V rms winding gives 14.1 V peak and a 28.3 V doubler, not 20 V.
Forgetting diode drops: each pair costs one Vd, so a quadrupler with 0.7 V diodes loses 2.8 V even at no load.
Expecting the output to hold at 100 mA; the cascade sags and ripples long before that.
Assuming ripple is at 2f; the half-wave cascade ripples at f, and only the bridge doubler gives 2f.
Under-rating capacitors: C1 sits at Vp, not 2Vp; D1 must withstand 2Vp reverse. Doubler output C2 sits at 2Vp; in an n-pair ladder the last capacitor sees n·Vp.

quiz.q: What is the no-load DC output of a half-wave doubler fed with peak Vp?
Why does the second diode see about 2Vp?
quiz.a: C1 is charged to Vp and sits in series with the source, so source and C1 add on the next half-cycle.

quiz.q: A 12 V peak source feeds an ideal quadrupler. Give the output, then repeat with Vd = 0.7 V.
A 10 V rms transformer feeds an ideal doubler. Find the no-load output.
Why does the cascade output fall faster under load than a bridge rectifier with the same capacitor?
quiz.a: Charge is delivered once per cycle, so ripple is at f not 2f, and current passes through n diodes in series; effective source resistance is larger, so sag and ripple are larger.

quiz.q: A student measures 26 V from a quadrupler fed by 10 V peak with 0.7 V diodes. Is that consistent with theory?
quiz.a: No. The no-load value is 40 − 2.8 = 37.2 V; 26 V means a heavy load or a measurement under load.

quiz.q: Which capacitor in the ladder must be rated above 2Vp?
quiz.a: C2, the output capacitor of the doubler (the output capacitor of the ladder in general). C1 holds only Vp; D1 must withstand 2Vp reverse.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cockcroft–Walton columns set megavolt bias in accelerators. The same charge pump sits inside flash memory. Modern versions switch at kHz to MHz to shrink capacitors; charge-pump ICs make negative or boosted rails.
